newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac offers little in interview to gloomy France.
newsitem.headline: Chirac offers little in interview to gloomy France.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac was criticised on Friday for offering too little in a two-hour television interview but his allies praised his courage for sticking to his policies despite growing public discontent.
In his first major interview since July, Chirac pledged late on Thursday to press ahead with austerity policies and European integration.
He also ruled out a cabinet reshuffle and said he would keep his trust in Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has become the least popular premier in modern French history.
"Is that all?", read the front page headline of the left-leaning daily Liberation, which summed up a general feeling in the press that Chirac had no miracle cure for gloom in France.
But the president's right-wing allies applauded his performance before a panel of tough-questioning reporters in the Elysee Palace.
"The president lived up to expectations," Defence Minister Charles Millon told French radio. "He refused the temptation of conservatism and the inevitability of decline."
Juppe said Chirac had expressed "a great ambition for a strong, generous and united France".
The conservative daily Le Figaro wrote Chirac had given a "second wind" to his rule and hailed him for saying he would reform the judiciary.
Chirac's only major new announcement was that he had told the government to set up a commission to strengthen the independence of prosecutors and bolster the presumption of innocence for suspects.

Chirac sought to persuade the French that the country was on the right track and that he had not forgotten his 1995 campaign promises such as war on unemployment, which has since risen to a record 12.6 percent.
But left-wing politicians were not impressed.

"Jacques Chirac...stuck to the course of a policy that doesn't work," Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande said while former Socialist minister Jack Lang said he did not agree with Chirac's vision of French society.

"He said the French were conservative but they're not," said Lang after Chirac blamed French people for being too resistant to change. "It's our political and economic rulers who are, at least most of them," Lang added.

Chirac made a strong defence of a planned single European currency from 1999 and the budget rigour needed to qualify for it, saying the euro was vital to revive France's economy and to give Europe the power to challenge U.S. "hegemony".

And he insisted a devaluation suggested by government allies including former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing would be disastrous -- saying it would break the Franco-German alliance at the heart of the European Union.
Chirac said he believed the EU would reach agreement, perhaps during this week's Dublin summit, on a "stability pact" on budgetary discipline in the future euro currency zone.

Grilled at length for the first time since he came to office in 1995 about suspected political kickbacks and sleaze probes into political parties including his own, Chirac said: "Probes must be carried out to the end and punishment must be all the more exemplary as it concerns people in positions of power."
He said the government should continue cutting taxes, especially income tax, as part of fiscal reform.
The popular newspaper Aujourd'hui said Chirac's interview failed to comfort worried French people.
"The goal was to give lost and discouraged Frenchmen new reasons to have hope in the future," wrote Aujourd'hui's columnist Dominique de Montvalon. "That goal was not reached."
